value: The conjecture-making stage of mathematical practice, and whether a supervised model plus attribution can guide it.
Computers have generated mathematical data for decades - can a learned model do the harder thing and help a mathematician see which relationships are worth conjecturing?
A framework - hypothesise a relation, learn it, attribute it, conjecture a closed form - demonstrated by two genuinely new results in different areas of pure mathematics.

quote: We propose a framework for augmenting the standard mathematician’s toolkit with powerful pattern recognition and interpretation methods from machine learning and demonstrate its value and generality by showing how it led us to two fundamental new discoveries, one in topology and another in representation theory.

We propose a process of using machine learning to discover potential patterns and relations between mathematical objects, understanding them with attribution techniques and using these observations to guide intuition and propose conjectures.

One of the central drivers of mathematical progress is the discovery of patterns and formulation of useful conjectures: statements that are suspected to be true but have not been proven to hold in all cases.

value: The proposed machine-learning framework produced genuinely new mathematics in two unrelated fields: a knot-theoretic connection between algebraic and geometric invariants, and a candidate resolution of a long-open conjecture in representation theory.
quote: In this work we have demonstrated a framework for mathematicians to use machine learning that has led to mathematical insight across two distinct disciplines: one of the first connections between the algebraic and geometric structure of knots and a proposed resolution to a long-standing open conjecture in representation theory.

value: Salient-subgraph analysis in the representation-theory case led to the discovery that a Bruhat interval decomposes into a hypercube plus a graph isomorphic to an interval in the smaller symmetric group.
quote: Considering this observation led us to the discovery that there is a natural decomposition of an interval into two parts—a hypercube induced by one set of extremal edges and a graph isomorphic to an interval in S N −1 .

value: This decomposition yields a proved theorem: every Bruhat interval admits a canonical hypercube decomposition from which the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial can be computed directly.
quote: Every Bruhat interval admits a canonical hypercube decomposition along its extremal reflections, from which the KL polynomial is directly computable.

value: Computational testing suggested the stronger claim that any hypercube decomposition, not just the canonical one, recovers the correct KL polynomial.
quote: Remarkably, further tests suggested that all hypercube decompositions correctly determine the KL polynomial.
